title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1RC0RE_1LD0RB_1RE0LC_1RA0LE_0RC---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1RC0RE_1LD0RB_1RE0LC_1RA0LE_0RC---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open; heuristically the machine does not halt. The tape is a queue of blocks (01)^k of sizes 4j − 2 with single-cell cursors travelling through it; all local rules are proved in Lean. The form of the tape does not exclude a halt: a tape of that form that halts is proved in Lean. An exact accelerated simulator (its jumps validated, not proved) runs 105000 steps without a halt. In that run the dangerous shape (three cursor cells 1 side by side) appeared nine times, and each time the birth of a cursor that would have left it standing was still at least M/2 visits away, M of the order of the square root of the step count (7,038 visits the first time, more than 10196 afterwards). No closed invariant is known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 77,847 cells have been visited and 38,670 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.559).

claims.title: Tape structure
claims.text: With a = 01 and b = 00110, the tape at each visit of the right end is 1 a (b a^2)^q followed by a list of blocks a^k separated by b, with single cursor cells in between (q = 127 at 1011 steps, 16,418,839 at 1018: a visit with no cursor on the tape inserts one b a^2 at the left). The block sizes that persist are 14, 62, 254, 1022, 4094, …, that is 4j − 2, each four times the previous plus 6.

claims.title: The local rules of the queue
claims.text: With a = 01, b = 00110 and the head in state B at the right end. Feeding: L a^(k+1) c a^m b a^(n+2) 0 B> becomes L a^k c' a^(m+4) b a^n 0 B> (the cursor c moves one a left and flips, the block after it gets 4, the end block pays 2; without a separator the end block gets 2). Crossing a separator in two visits: b 0 → 0 a 1 1 a b → 0 a^6 b, and b 1 a^m → 0 0 a^(m+5) → 1 a b a^m. Birth: when the end block is empty the last separator becomes a new cursor and the old one stays where it is. All for all sizes and every tape to the left.

claims.title: A queue of blocks of size 4^j - 2
claims.text: A cursor that walks through a block of k copies leaves 4k (plus 6 at a separator) behind it, which gives the persistent sizes 2, 14, 62, 254, 1022, ... The numbers of equal blocks persist from one size to the next (1264, 127 and 258 copies sit at sizes 254, 1022, 16382 at 2×10<sup>15</sup> steps and at 16382, 65534, 1048574 at 10<sup>18</sup>): a self-similar counter. Observed; the global schedule of the cursors is not understood.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>18</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: py/qsim.py is an exact simulator with macro rules for a^n, b and (b a^n)^q, plus jumps: when the same tape shape recurs with constant changes of the counts for 4 periods, many periods are applied at once and the next one is checked. Without jumps it agrees with a cell-by-cell simulator at every visit of the right end tested (6,000 visits, 5.3×107 steps); with jumps it agrees with the run without jumps at every visit up to 3×1010 steps. It reaches 1018 steps in 160 s without a halt (3,304,842 visits simulated one by one, 127,033 jumps). The jumps are validated, not proved. (An earlier accelerated run, rsim.py, reached 4.61×1014 steps.)

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>5000</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: go/fsim.go is the same exact rope engine in Go with big integers, plus exact bulk feeding (all visits of one feeding run at once, with their step count) and periodic jumps over whole visits, each validated by the period after it. Checked: the plain engine against a cell-by-cell simulator of the table at each of the 38,111 visits of the first 109 steps; bulk feeding against the plain engine at 11,838 visits up to 1.1×1012 steps; jumps against bulk feeding alone up to 1.1×1016 steps; runs with other settings give the same tape at every common visit between 10300 and 10400 steps. It reaches 105000 steps without a halt in 29 minutes (43,426,874 visits stopped at, 12,064 jumps, no rollback). The jumps are validated, not proved.

claims.title: A tape of the block form that halts
claims.text: The tape 1 a b a 0 a 1 1 1 0 a^22 0 B> (blocks, one separator, cursor cells) halts after 213 steps: three cursor cells 1 side by side, with the next cursor arriving as a 0 directly right of them, is the halting shape. So “blocks, separators and cursors” is not an invariant that excludes halting. This is not a statement about the run from blank tape.

claims.title: How close the run from blank tape came
claims.text: The halting shape needs (1) a birth while a cursor is half way across a separator (0 a 1 1 a b), (2) a later cursor reaching that place, which gives 1 1 1 for one visit, and (3) a birth at exactly that visit. In the first 1018 steps there are 124 births; (1) happened once (birth 22, step 7.08×108), (2) followed at step 1.057×1011, the only visit among 3,304,842 simulated one by one with three cursor cells 1 side by side; (3) did not happen: the end block held 14,076 copies, not 0. With of the order 109 visits and 124 births in 1018 steps, a random visit is a birth with chance about 10−7; the real schedule is determined, not random, and not understood. To 105000 steps (go/fsim.go): 51,981 births seen, 74 of them half way across a separator, and nine visits with 1 1 1. At each of the nine the end block b a^M 0 was far from empty, so the next birth was at least M/2 visits away: 7,038 visits at the first, then numbers of 197, 867, 1359, 1636, 1766, 1784, 1860 and 2496 digits (steps about 10394 to 104994); M mod 8 takes the values 0, 2, 4 and 6.

claims.title: A probabilistic estimate: it does not halt
claims.text: A triple ends in a halt only if a birth falls on its visit, that is if the active cursor's end block, which holds M copies (M of the order of the square root of the step count), runs out exactly there. If that moment fell at random within the cursor's life the chance would be about 2/M: about 1/7000 for the first triple, below 10<sup>-196</sup> for each later one. Triples come about once in 550 decades of the step count (nine in 5000), so the chance that any later one ends in a halt is below 10<sup>-2490</sup>. The schedule is deterministic, so this is an estimate, not a proof; a halt by a structured coincidence that the random model does not see is not excluded.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. A proof of non-halting has to show that a birth never falls on the visit at which three cursor cells 1 stand together (or that the next cursor then arrives as a 1); a proof of halting has to find when it does. Both need the global schedule of the cursors: the counter of equal blocks as an exact recurrence. The sibling 1RB1RF_0RC0RE_0RD1RA_1LE0LA_1LB0LD_0RD--- has an outside proof in review that it halts; that proof is not in this repository, so its mechanism could not be compared.

claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LE_1RC0LB_1RD1RF_1RE0RB_1LA0RD_0RE--- up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each. The same table as 1RB0LE_1LC0RA_1LD0RC_1LE1LF_1LA0LC_0LA--- up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

python3 holdouts/1RB1RF_1RC0RE_1LD0RB_1RE0LC_1RA0LE_0RC---/py/qsim_check.py jumps 3e8     # jumps on against jumps off

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but probably not. The tape is a queue of blocks 0101… separated by a five-cell marker, and single odd cells (cursors) travel through it, making every block four times longer. The machine can only stop if three such cursors pile up at exactly the moment a new one is born. In 105000 steps the pile-up happened nine times, never at that moment.

facts.text: Feeding, crossing a separator and the birth of a cursor, proved in Lean for all block sizes.
Three cursor cells 1 with a cursor 0 arriving: a tape of the block form that halts (213 steps), proved in Lean.
No halt in an exact accelerated simulator (validated against plain simulation; jumps not proved).
Visits with three cursor cells 1 side by side in 10<sup>5000</sup> steps; at each, the next birth was at least 7,038 visits (later more than 10<sup>196</sup>) away.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: Blocks, separators and cursors
html: Write a for 01 and b for 00110. Each time the head arrives at the right end of the tape (a visit), the tape is a row of blocks a^k separated by b, with a few single cells, 0 or 1, in between: the cursors. A cursor is a place where the regular beat 0101… skips; the rightmost one is the active one.

One visit moves the active cursor one a to the left and flips it. The block behind it grows by 4 copies of a, and the block at the very end of the tape pays 2. So a cursor that walks through a block of k copies leaves 4k behind: with the 6 extra copies it picks up when it crosses a separator, sizes go 2 → 14 → 62 → 254 → …, each 4k + 6, that is 4j − 2.

Crossing a separator takes two visits (b 0 → 0 a 1 1 a b → 0 a^6 b). And when the end block has nothing left to pay, the last separator itself turns into a new cursor (a birth); the cursor that was active simply stays where it is until a later cursor runs into it.
All of this is proved in Lean for all block sizes (lean/Rules.lean). After 1018 steps the tape holds, among others, 1,299,680 blocks of 14, 47,575 blocks of 1022 and 258 blocks of 1,048,574.

sections.heading: Three cursors in a row, at the wrong moment
html: The machine stops only if state A reads two 1s in a row. Inside the queue that happens in one situation: three cursor cells 1 1 1 stand side by side and the next cursor arrives directly to their right as a 0. Lean proves that this tape, which has exactly the form the run keeps, halts after 213 steps:
1 a b a 0 a 1 1 1 0 a^22 0 B>
How could the run get there? Three things must line up:

1. a birth happens while a cursor is half way across a separator, leaving 0 a 1 1 a b behind;
  2. a later cursor reaches that place: for exactly one visit the tape reads 1 1 1 there, and one visit later 0 a 1 a^14, harmless;
  3. a birth happens at exactly that one visit, so the three 1s are left standing for the next cursor.

In the first 1018 steps step 1 happened once, at step 7.08×108, and step 2 followed at step 1.057×1011. Step 3 did not: the end block, which pays 2 copies at every visit and whose emptying is what triggers a birth, still held 14,076 copies, so the next birth was 7,038 visits away.

A faster simulator, written for this machine, follows the run to 105000 steps, a number with five thousand digits. It does not simulate every step: it recognizes stretches where the same thing happens over and over (a cursor walking through a long block) and does them in one arithmetic move, and every shortcut it takes is checked against the step-by-step machine. Three 1s in a row turned up nine times. Each time, the next birth was far away:

near missaround stepvisits to the next birth
110117,038
210394a 197-digit number
3101735866 digits
4–8102720 to 1037231358 to 1860 digits
91049942496 digits

The miss is always about as large as the tape is long, which is about the square root of the step count. If the moment of birth were a roll of the dice, the first near miss had a 1 in 7,000 chance of ending the run and every later one less than 1 in 10196: by that count the machine runs forever. But the schedule is not dice; the machine's sibling (same kind of queue, sizes 4j) has an outside proof, in review, that it does halt. The question stays open until someone works out the exact timetable of the cursors.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB0LE_1RC0LB_1RD1RF_1RE0RB_1LA0RD_0RE---: rename A→C, B→D, C→E, D→A, E→B, F→F; it is this table started in state D
  • 1RB0LE_1LC0RA_1LD0RC_1LE1LF_1LA0LC_0LA---: rename A→D, B→E, C→A, D→B, E→C, F→F and exchange left and right; it is this table started in state C, in a mirror

summary: Block queue with cursors (block sizes 4^j - 2): all local rules proved in Lean; a tape of the same form that halts is proved in Lean; an exact accelerated simulator runs 10^5000 steps without a halt, the halting coincidence was missed nine times by margins near the square root of the step count; open, heuristically non-halting.
